Control the jump-off of any model

Source: R/model-anchor.R
anchored.Rd

Forecasts of most models start from their fitted rates in the last observed year. Where the fit misses the level of the last years (for example after a recent change of trend), the forecast starts with a step away from the observations. anchored() wraps any model specification and moves the start of its forecasts to the observed level, per age and stratum. With the defaults this is the jump-off adjustment of Lee and Miller (2001): the forecasts start from the observed rates of the last training year and keep this offset in every forecast year.

Usage

anchored(
  spec,
  to = c("observed", "smoothed"),
  years = 1,
  decay = Inf,
  shrink = FALSE
)

Arguments

spec

A model specification.

to

"observed" or "smoothed".

years

Number of last training years whose deaths define the offset (default 1, the last training year; see above for the averages of Stoeldraijer et al. 2018).

decay

Years over which the offset fades out (default Inf: constant).

shrink

Shrink offsets of ages with few deaths towards the mean of their stratum (default FALSE).

Value

A model specification. The fitted object has the offsets in $anchor$offset ([age, stratum], log scale).

Details

  1. the offset is the log ratio of observed to fitted deaths, summed over the last years training years (to = "observed": the rates before smoothing; to = "smoothed": the rates after preprocessing, which differs when the pipeline smooths);

  2. with shrink = TRUE, offsets of ages with few deaths are shrunk towards the mean offset of their stratum (see below);

  3. the forecast draws are multiplied by exp(offset * w(h)), where the weight w(h) falls linearly from 1 at the first forecast year to 0 after decay years (decay = Inf keeps the offset; decay = 0 leaves the model's own jump-off).

The defaults years = 1, decay = Inf, shrink = FALSE give, for any model, the observed jump-off of Lee-Carter models (lee_carter(jump_off = "observed")). The offset multiplies every draw of a cell by the same factor, so it moves the forecast distribution of the log rates without changing its width. Models that have no fitted rates (random walks, time series per age) start from the observed rates already and are left unchanged; in an ensemble() each draw is anchored with the offset of the component it comes from, which moves the components relative to each other and can change the width of the mixture. For reconciled() models the bottom strata are anchored and the aggregates recomputed, so the draws stay coherent. mt_jump_off() reports the step between the last observed or fitted year and the first forecast year.

Jump-off options of Stoeldraijer et al. (2018). The jump-off rates are the rates of the last year of the fitting period, the jump-off year. Stoeldraijer et al. compare six options for the Lee-Carter model (their names in quotes):

  • "model values", the fitted rates of the jump-off year (Lee and Carter 1992): the model itself, without anchored() (or decay = 0);

  • "last observed values" (Lee and Miller 2001): anchored() with its defaults, for any model; for Lee-Carter also lee_carter(jump_off = "observed");

  • "average n years observed" (n = 2 to 5): lee_carter(jump_off = "observed", jump_off_years = n), as the paper defines it: the mean of the observed log rates of the last n years, with the index 0 at the midpoint of these years. anchored(years = n) is a package-specific variant for any model (reference unknown): its offset is the log ratio of the observed to the fitted deaths of these years, so the forecast also keeps the change of the fitted rates from these years to the last year.

They call a forecast accurate if its out-of-sample errors in historical data are small (mean absolute error of the forecast life expectancy at 65 one and five years ahead), and robust if it changes little when one more year of data is added (standard deviation of the changes of the forecast life expectancy at 65 in 2020 between successive fitting periods). In eight Western European countries the last observed values were the most accurate for most countries and an average of observed years the most robust; the more years averaged, the more robust and the less accurate the forecast. The model values were the most accurate where the model fitted the last years well. They recommend moving from the most accurate jump-off in the first forecast year to the most robust one by the fifth (Appendix 6, without a formula for the weights). Where the last observed values are the most accurate and the model values the most robust, anchored(decay = 4) does this: the weight of the observed offset falls linearly from 1 in the first forecast year to 0 in the fifth (the linear weights are package-specific). The filtered jump-off of De Jong and Tickle (2006) is lee_carter(jump_off = "filtered").

Package-specific options (reference unknown). Starting from the observed rates of one year carries their random variation into every forecast year, which matters where deaths are few. The other settings are package-specific: averaging the offset over the last years years (see above), fading it out over decay years (forecasts more than decay years ahead are then those of the model itself, and during the fade the offsets add a small apparent trend) and shrinking it (shrink = TRUE). The shrinkage is empirical Bayes within each stratum: the offset \(r_x\) of age \(x\) has the approximate Poisson sampling variance \(v_x = 1/D_x\), where \(D_x\) is the number of deaths in the last years (at least 0.5); the variance \(\tau^2\) of the true offsets between the ages of the stratum is estimated with the moment estimator of DerSimonian and Laird (1986); and each offset becomes \(\hat\mu + \tau^2 / (\tau^2 + v_x) (r_x - \hat\mu)\), where \(\hat\mu\) is the mean offset weighted by \(1 / (\tau^2 + v_x)\).

Anchoring helps where the fitted rates of the last year are far from the observed level; where the model's own jump-off is already close to it, anchoring changes little. The vignette "Where a forecast starts: the jump-off" shows the effect in a backtest.

References

Stoeldraijer L, van Duin C, van Wissen L, Janssen F (2018). Comparing strategies for matching mortality forecasts to the most recently observed data: exploring the trade-off between accuracy and robustness. Genus 74: 16. doi:10.1186/s41118-018-0041-y

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87(419): 659-671.

Lee R, Miller T (2001). Evaluating the performance of the Lee-Carter method for forecasting mortality. Demography 38(4): 537-549.

De Jong P, Tickle L (2006). Extending Lee-Carter mortality forecasting. Mathematical Population Studies 13(1): 1-18. doi:10.1080/08898480500452109

DerSimonian R, Laird N (1986). Meta-analysis in clinical trials. Controlled Clinical Trials 7(3): 177-188.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(anchored(lee_carter()), x)
summary(as.vector(fit$anchor$offset))
#>       Min.    1st Qu.     Median       Mean    3rd Qu.       Max. 
#> -0.4028109 -0.0241849  0.0004603 -0.0013737  0.0269568  0.2285328 
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
mt_jump_off(fc)
#>       sex  label observed   fitted forecast step_observed step_fitted
#>    <char> <char>    <num>    <num>    <num>         <num>       <num>
#> 1: female female 55.95597 55.95828 56.06028    0.10431465   0.1020055
#> 2:   male   male 51.16230 51.17137 51.25410    0.09180217   0.0827333
# package-specific: the mean offset of three years, fading out over ten years
fit3 <- mt_fit(anchored(lee_carter(), years = 3, decay = 10, shrink = TRUE), x)
